Ford’s smash-hit Mustang needed legitimate racetrack credibility to humble Chevrolet’s Corvette in SCCA B-Production, so Lee Iacocca enlisted Le Mans winner Carroll Shelby to homologate 100 stripped-out bruisers for 1965.

That iconic first-generation Shelby Mustang stayed in production across five model years, from 1965 through 1969—wrapping up in 1970 with 789 re-VINed 1969 leftovers—accounting for just 13,912 total cars, including roughly 6,901 GT350s.
Across those 5 production years, the GT350’s powertrain recipe shifted with Detroit’s appetites.

Production quadrupled from 562 units in 1965 to 2,378 cars, spanning 1,365 street models (starting with 252 carryover builds), roughly 1,000 Hertz GT350H Rent-a-Racers, 4 drag cars, executive convertibles, and prototypes.

On track, 1966 sealed Shelby’s legend: Walt Hane captured SCCA’s B-Production crown, while Jerry Titus won the Riverside finale in a Shelby-prepped Mustang to clinch Ford’s inaugural Trans-Am Manufacturers Championship.

Teen Got New 1966 Shelby GT350, Policeman Bought It To Keep Him out of Jail, Family had It 50 Years
55 photos
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150
Moparheads typically stick to their guns, and don’t venture outside the Pentastar orbit, lest they commit sacrilege of the highest order. Unless there’s a very, very good reason for a multi-universe detour. So, what would it take for a car hunter who lives and breathes Plymouth-Dodge to even consider looking at other Detroit giants? A 1966 Shelby Mustang GT350, owned by the same family for over 50 years.
True garage finds are supposed to be extinct in today’s hyper-connected collector market, yet every so often a dust-caked thoroughbred crawls out of hiding to prove the barn-find gods still appreciate good theater.
Troy Bergeron—normally a die-hard Pentastar evangelist, and also the man in charge for Mopars5150’s YouTube channel coast to coast adventures—pointed his rig toward Redding, California, to scoop up an outrageously solid 1966 Shelby GT350 that spent nearly 40 years disassembled inside a Denver garage.
Ford assembled the K-code fastback in San Jose, California, on March 17 and 18, 1966, before shipping it to Shelby American’s Los Angeles International Airport facility. There, Carroll Shelby’s crew transformed it into serial number SFM6S1578—Candyapple Red with white Rally stripes, a 4-speed manual, and an AM radio—and shipped it to a Littleton, Colorado Ford dealer, which relocated the antenna rearward to cure ignition static.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 From that showroom, the ownership chain reads like muscle-era folklore. The first owner was a Denver teenager who street-raced the fastback relentlessly, earning a thick stack of tickets from one local police officer, Mr. Callahan. After warning the boy’s parents to sell the Shelby or pay their son regular visits to the county jail, Officer Callahan promptly bought the GT350 himself, launching roughly 50 years of Callahan family stewardship—and immediately handing the keys to his wife.
Ford purists should brace themselves for what happened next. Mrs. Callahan detested Candyapple Red and white stripes so intensely that she had the Shelby resprayed a loud, Mopar-esque Sublime lime green, then daily-drove it through Colorado winters on mud-and-snow tires that still accompany the car today. Sons Mike and Tim Callahan grew up bouncing around the back seat until Mike turned 16 or 17, when his mother passed the neon-green pony down to him.
Appalled by the radioactive shade, Mike immediately repainted the fastback red again, leaving zero surviving photographs of its green phase—only stubborn lime overspray lurking along the firewall, rockers, and engine bay. By the mid-to-late 1980s, with roughly 78,000 miles logged, Mike stripped the Shelby completely apart inside his Denver garage.
Worse, he sent the original VIN-stamped 289 block to a local machine shop that went belly-up, losing it forever while the car slumbered for nearly 40 years.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 After Mike passed away, younger brother Tim Callahan inherited the buried jigsaw puzzle and finally decided to sell. For five years, Tim’s Colorado neighbor had mentioned the disassembled red Shelby to Conrad Tona of Redding, California, mistakenly calling it a 1967 model. When Conrad forwarded the lead to his longtime friend Troy Bergeron of Mopars5150, the seasoned car hunter realized from the photos it was an authentic 1966 GT350—the exact dream car Conrad had chased his whole life.
Being a stand-up friend, Troy stepped back so Conrad—hilariously a Ford die-hard cursed with a surname begging for a Dodge Daytona pun—could become the third owner. Conrad and his father-in-law hauled the car out of Tim’s Denver garage, mocked it together in Redding, and verified 18 pages of records with 1966 Shelby registrar Howard Pardee—initially suggesting stripe-delete until white paint and one invoice note confirmed factory Rally stripes—before selling it to Troy a year later.
What makes this Denver survivor jaw-dropping is its preservation. Despite braving Rocky Mountain slush, the floorpans are spotless, the roof is undented, and only one tiny rust blister marks the steel. Beyond a 1960s brazed right-rear quarter repair using original Ford metal without harming the outer wheelhouse, it wears every glorious LAX factory quirk.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 The discarded Ford door tag, riveted Shelby VIN over San Jose’s stamp, crooked decal, jagged quarter-vent cuts, crude traction-bar welds, blue adjustable shocks, and one missing shock-tower washer.
Its surviving parts stash is an archaeologist’s dream: five original Shelby wheels, close-ratio 4-speed , 9-inch axle, rear drums, dated Ray Brown seat belts, dash-drilled tachometer, original interior and exhaust, white Tri-Y headers, stamped Cobra intake and oil pan, K-code heads, Brinell-tested crank, 3/8-inch-bolt rods, heavy-duty balancer, dual-point distributor, and 6-blade water pump.
Only the factory shifter, a $2,500 Holley carburetor, and the lost block vanished; Conrad added a date-correct K-code block, which Troy refuses to restamp while hunting the original.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 To grasp why enthusiasts practically swoon over a stripped 1966 fastback, rewind to 1964. Ford’s smash-hit Mustang needed legitimate racetrack credibility to humble Chevrolet’s Corvette in SCCA B-Production, so Lee Iacocca enlisted Le Mans winner Carroll Shelby to homologate 100 stripped-out bruisers for 1965.
That iconic first-generation Shelby Mustang stayed in production across five model years, from 1965 through 1969—wrapping up in 1970 with 789 re-VINed 1969 leftovers—accounting for just 13,912 total cars, including roughly 6,901 GT350s.
Across those 5 production years, the GT350’s powertrain recipe shifted with Detroit’s appetites. From 1965 through 1967, it ran Ford’s 289-cubic-inch (4.7-liter) K-code V8, before pivoting to a 250-hp (253-PS) 302-cubic-inch (4.9-liter) V8 in 1968 and a 290-hp (294-PS) 351-cubic-inch (5.8-liter) Windsor for 1969 and 1970, with a Paxton supercharger optional from 1966 to 1968.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Transmissions spanned 1965’s Borg-Warner T-10 4-speed, Ford’s Toploader 4-speed, the C4 3-speed automatic, and 1969–1970’s cast-iron FMX 3-speed automatic. Yet 1966 transformed the GT350 from a bare-knuckle homologation special into a pop-culture juggernaut. Production quadrupled from 562 units in 1965 to 2,378 cars, spanning 1,365 street models (starting with 252 carryover builds), roughly 1,000 Hertz GT350H Rent-a-Racers, 4 drag cars, executive convertibles, and prototypes.
Because Hertz ordered about 915 C4 automatics against just 85 manuals while retail buyers overwhelmingly picked sticks, overall 1966 outpu t split nearly evenly, with 4-speeds holding a narrow edge.
Unlike 1965’s Wimbledon White-only dictate, 1966 opened five factory liveries—Wimbledon White, Candyapple Red, Sapphire Blue, Ivy Green, and Raven Black—with optional Le Mans stripes and Hertz’s iconic black-and-gold scheme.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Underneath, Shelby promoted Ford’s 271-hp (275-PS), 312-lb-ft (423-Nm) K-code 289 to 306 hp (310 PS) and 329 lb-ft (446 Nm) using a Cobra aluminum high-rise intake, 715-cfm Holley carburetor (Autolite 4100 on automatics), cast-aluminum Cobra valve covers and oil pan, and tubular Tri-Y headers.
Beyond extra muscle, Shelby added an export brace, Monte Carlo bar, beefier anti-roll bar, adjustable shocks, traction bars, metallic-lined brakes, proportioning valve, Plexiglas quarter windows, side brake scoops, and a scooped hood, while adding street civility via rear-exit exhaust, an underhood battery, and a fold-down rear seat.
At a $4,428 base price, options included the C4 automatic, Rally stripes, AM radio, Detroit Locker, upgrade wheels, and a $517-plus Paxton supercharger ordered on just 11 factory cars.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Period Car and Driver tests backed up the hype, clocking 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 6.6 to 6.9 seconds, the quarter-mile in 15.2 seconds at 93 mph (150 kph), and nearly 140 mph (225 kph) flat out. On track, 1966 sealed Shelby’s legend: Walt Hane captured SCCA’s B-Production crown, while Jerry Titus won the Riverside finale in a Shelby-prepped Mustang to clinch Ford’s inaugural Trans-Am Manufacturers Championship.
That championship DNA makes this red-over-Sublime-over-red Denver time capsule pure American motorsport theater. Between a ticket-happy Colorado cop, a wife bold enough to paint Carroll Shelby’s finest in Mopar lime green, 40 years of silent garage hibernation, and untouched factory quirks, SFM6S1578 has soul to spare.
Now headed to Mopars5150’s dealership, this Candyapple Red 4-speed icon just needs a dedicated restorer, one pricey Holley carburetor, and maybe one miracle call from Denver.
